findings.title: Normal operational messages logged at ERROR level
findings.body: Lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579 all use `r.log.Error(...)` to log routine cleanup progress (e.g., how many IDs were fetched, how many rows were affected). These are not errors—they represent normal successful operation. In production, this will flood the error log with thousands of entries per cleanup cycle, making it harder to identify real errors and potentially triggering false alerts on error-rate monitoring. These should be `r.log.Debug` or `r.log.Info`.

findings.title: Cleanup interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without explanation
findings.body: The ticker interval is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, causing all cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) to run 10× more frequently. This increases database load across all cleanup operations, not just annotations. If the intent is only to run annotation cleanup more often to compensate for smaller batch sizes, this change is overly broad. The PR description does not justify this change.

findings.title: SQLite parameter limit check uses configured batch size instead of actual ID count
findings.body: The condition `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` checks the configured batch size rather than `len(ids)`. If the batch size is configured above 999 but a particular batch returns fewer than 999 IDs (e.g., near the end of cleanup), the code still inlines the values into the SQL string instead of using parameterized queries. While functionally correct, this is inconsistent: on non-SQLite databases the same small batch would use parameters. More importantly, if a future database introduces a similar parameter limit, this pattern would need to be replicated. The check should be `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`.

findings.title: cutoffDate is interpolated directly into SQL string without parameterization
findings.body: The `cutoffDate` integer is embedded into the SQL condition via `fmt.Sprintf` (`created < %v`). While the value is internally computed and not user-controlled, this bypasses the database driver's parameter binding. If the `fetchIDs`/`deleteByIDs` pattern is extended in the future to accept externally-influenced conditions, this pattern becomes a SQL injection vector. Using a parameterized query (passing cutoffDate as a bind parameter) would be safer and more consistent with the rest of the codebase.
